# EDA Findings (generated by eda.py from the actual data)

## Research questions and answers

**Q1. How complete is the data?** The dataset has 891 rows and 21 columns after cleaning (the raw file has 15 columns). Columns with missing values: age (177, 19.9%), embarked (2, 0.2%), deck (688, 77.2%), embark_town (2, 0.2%). There are 107 exact duplicate rows, which were kept because the data has no ID column to prove they are copies.

**Q2. What was the overall survival rate?** 38.4%.

**Q3. Did survival differ by sex?** Survival rate by sex: female 74.2%, male 18.9%.

**Q4. Did survival differ by passenger class?** class 1: 63.0%, class 2: 47.3%, class 3: 24.2%. Class and sex together (survival rate %): class 1: female 97%, male 37%; class 2: female 92%, male 16%; class 3: female 50%, male 14%.

**Q5. Did age matter?** Among passengers with a known age, the highest survival rate was Child (0-12) (58.0%, n=69) and the lowest was Senior (61+) (22.7%, n=22). Passengers whose age is missing survived at 29.4%.

**Q6. Did family size matter?** Looking only at family sizes with at least 30 passengers, the highest survival rate was for family size 3 (57.8%) and the lowest for family size 1 (30.4%). Larger family sizes have very few passengers, so their rates are unreliable.

**Q7. What do fares look like?** Median fare by class: class 1 = 60.29, class 2 = 14.25, class 3 = 8.05. 116 passengers have unusually high fares (IQR rule), and 15 passengers have a fare of 0.

**Q8. Which numeric variable has the strongest linear link with survival?** pclass (correlation -0.34).

## Limitations
- The Titanic dataset is a well-known teaching dataset (a demonstration dataset). It is real historical data but it is not a model of any current business problem.
- Age is missing for a large part of the passengers, so age results are based on a subset.
- Correlation and group differences show association, not cause and effect.
- The data comes from the seaborn-data copy of the dataset and has no passenger names or ticket numbers, so duplicates cannot be verified.
- Small groups (for example large families) give unstable percentages.
